screens.title: What is AWS CodeBuild?
screens.narratorSegment: Start with a simple claim: CodeBuild is a fully managed continuous integration service that runs your build commands and produces artifacts without provisioning build servers. That means you describe what to do in a buildspec. yml and CodeBuild runs it in a managed environment or a custom Docker image you provide. A concrete example: you commit a Node. js project to CodeCommit and configure CodeBuild to run npm install, npm run build, and npm test; CodeBuild executes those commands and uploads the output to S3. A common misconception is that CodeBuild supplies persistent state between builds. It does not — builds are ephemeral. To persist dependencies across builds you use the cache feature or an artifacts bucket. Another contrast: managed images provide common runtimes preinstalled, while custom images let you bake in specialized tools. Why this matters: choosing the right environment affects reproducibility and first-run failures. Key questions to ask when designing a build are what commands must run, where artifacts should go, and which IAM permissions are needed. Practice by writing a minimal buildspec. yml and running a single build — that will reveal whether your runtime and paths are correct. How would you make your first build deterministic?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: CodeBuild runs buildspec-driven commands in managed or custom environments and outputs artifacts to S3.

content.html:
Core Concept
What is CodeBuild?
A managed CI service that runs build commands, executes tests, and packages artifacts without you managing build servers.
Quick facts
  • Runs commands defined in buildspec.yml sequentially across phases.
  • Uses managed or custom Docker images as build environments.
  • Uploads artifacts to S3 and writes logs to CloudWatch Logs.
Key Takeaway

CodeBuild removes server maintenance and executes only the commands you define in buildspec.yml; use caches and artifacts to persist useful outputs between builds.

Analogy & Example
Think of CodeBuild as a chef that follows your recipe file. The recipe lists steps to fetch ingredients, prepare, cook, and plate. For a Node.js app, a recipe might install npm packages, run lint, build, and run tests.
Common misconception
Build environments are ephemeral. If you expect locally installed tools to persist between builds, you must bake them into a custom image or reinstall them in the install phase.
Check your understanding
Describe one advantage and one trade-off of using a custom Docker image versus a managed image for CodeBuild.

screens.title: Understanding buildspec.yml phases
screens.narratorSegment: The buildspec. yml is the instruction set CodeBuild follows. Treat it as a sequence of phases: install, pre_build, build, and post_build. Put runtime installs and dependency managers in install — for example, installing Node. js runtime or running npm install so subsequent steps can use installed packages. Use pre_build for validation steps such as linting or authentication actions. The build phase contains the core compile or package commands like npm run build or mvn package. Use post_build for tasks that prepare artifacts, run integration tests, or signal downstream systems. A concrete example: in a Node. js pipeline you would set runtime-versions. nodejs, run npm install in install, npm run lint in pre_build, npm run build in build, and npm test in post_build. A common mistake is placing dependency downloads in pre_build; if the runtime isn't present earlier, commands fail. Also be explicit with artifacts. base-directory so produced files end up where CodeBuild expects. Correctly placing steps reduces first-run failures and makes logs easier to interpret. What single change would you make if your tests fail because dependencies are missing? Understanding buildspec.yml phases means install tools and runtimes in install, run checks in pre_build, compile/package in build, and finalize artifacts or tests in post_build.. In practical terms, install, pre_build, build, and post_build — what belongs where. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Phase mapping
keyIdea.text: Install tools and runtimes in install, run checks in pre_build, compile/package in build, and finalize artifacts or tests in post_build.

content.html:
Process Flow
buildspec.yml phases
  1. install: install runtimes and dependencies needed by later steps.
  2. pre_build: validation, linting, or login actions before the main build.
  3. build: compile or package the application.
  4. post_build: run tests, prepare artifact metadata, or notify services.
Tip: wrong phase placement is a frequent cause of failures. Keep installs first so subsequent steps have required tools.
Example snippet
version: 0.2 phases: install: runtime-versions: nodejs: 18 commands: - echo "Installing dependencies..." - npm install pre_build: commands: - echo "Running linting..." - npm run lint build: commands: - echo "Building the application..." - npm run build post_build: commands: - echo "Running unit tests..." - npm test - echo "Build completed successfully!" artifacts: files: - '**/*' base-directory: 'dist' discard-paths: no cache: paths: - '/root/.npm/**'
This snippet demonstrates where to put runtime-versions, installs, and artifact configuration for a Node.js app.

screens.title: Node.js buildspec walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a practical Node. js buildspec and explain each section. The file starts with version: 0.2 then declares phases. Under install we set runtime-versions. nodejs to 18 and run npm install, which prepares node_modules for later steps. In pre_build we run lint to catch style issues early. The build phase runs npm run build to produce production-ready files, typically in a dist directory. Post_build runs tests, and if they succeed the artifacts block tells CodeBuild to collect files under base-directory: 'dist' and upload them to S3. Cache paths such as /root/. npm/** preserve npm packages between builds to reduce time and cost. A concrete example is the buildspec used in this chapter; it installs, lints, builds, tests, and caches npm. A frequent error is incorrect base-directory or glob patterns that exclude files; verify your build created the expected folder before trusting the artifact upload. Another trap is forgetting to add s3 permissions to the service role, leading to Access Denied when uploading artifacts. After running one build, inspect CloudWatch Logs to confirm each phase ran as intended. How will you validate the artifact contains the files you expect?

keyIdea.title: Concrete example
keyIdea.text: A Node.js buildspec installs dependencies, lints, builds into dist, runs tests, and caches npm packages to speed up future builds.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Node.js buildspec example
version: 0.2 phases: install: runtime-versions: nodejs: 18 commands: - echo "Installing dependencies..." - npm install pre_build: commands: - echo "Running linting..." - npm run lint build: commands: - echo "Building the application..." - npm run build post_build: commands: - echo "Running unit tests..." - npm test - echo "Build completed successfully!" artifacts: files: - '**/*' base-directory: 'dist' discard-paths: no cache: paths: - '/root/.npm/**'
This complete example demonstrates how runtime, commands, artifacts, and cache work together for a typical Node.js project.
Notes & Pitfalls
  • Ensure base-directory matches where the build produces files, otherwise artifacts will be empty.
  • Cache paths must point to absolute or consistent locations to be effective.
  • Runtime mismatch causes failed installs; pin runtime-versions explicitly when needed.
Key Takeaway

Write and test buildspec locally by running equivalent commands in a container to confirm paths and outputs before committing.

screens.title: Artifacts and Cache Explained
screens.narratorSegment: Artifacts and cache both persist data between steps or builds, but they serve different purposes. Artifacts are the final outputs you intend to deploy or store — packaged files uploaded to S3 after a successful build, defined via artifacts. files and a base-directory. Cache preserves intermediate dependencies or build outputs between runs to speed subsequent builds, for example caching /root/. npm to avoid re-downloading packages. Use artifacts when you need reproducible deployables; use cache to reduce build time and cost. A common mistake is treating cache as a replacement for artifacts. Cache is optional and may be pruned; artifacts are the canonical build outputs. Another frequent error is incorrect glob patterns in artifacts. files, which omit files from uploads. To validate, always inspect the build output directory before upload and check the S3 ZIP contents. If you see Access Denied uploading artifacts, check the CodeBuild service role for s3:PutObject permission scoped to the artifact bucket. Which files in your build should be artifacts and which should be cached? Artifacts and Cache Explained means artifacts = deployable outputs in s3; cache = performance optimization for dependency reuse between builds.. In practical terms, when to use artifacts, when to use cache, and common mistakes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Contrast
keyIdea.text: Artifacts = deployable outputs in S3; Cache = performance optimization for dependency reuse between builds.

content.html:
Comparison
Artifacts vs Cache
Artifacts (S3)
Final build outputs uploaded to S3. Defined with files and base-directory. Use for deployment packages.
Cache
Stores dependencies between builds, like npm packages, to reduce install time but is not a substitute for artifacts.
Validate by unzipping the artifact in S3 and confirming expected files. For cache, measure time saved across builds to confirm effectiveness.
Common mistakes
  • Wrong base-directory causing empty artifacts.
  • Glob patterns that exclude nested files you expected.
  • Assuming cache guarantees persistence; caches can be evicted and should be used only for speed.
Pro tip

Explicitly list artifact files or use a clean base-directory to guarantee predictable uploads.

screens.title: Choosing the build environment
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing an environment determines which runtimes and tools are available during a build. Managed images provide standard runtimes and are a quick way to get started. They are maintained by the provider and include common SDKs and tools. Custom Docker images let you preinstall exactly the toolchain your builds need, so builds start faster and behave identically across runs. In buildspec. yml you can also declare runtime-versions to pin language runtimes such as nodejs: 18 so commands run against a predictable interpreter. A concrete trade-off: managed images reduce maintenance but might lack niche tooling; custom images require you to build and host the image but give full control. Always test your build commands inside the chosen environment locally or in a container to catch missing tools early. Remember to document which image and runtime-version your project relies on so others can reproduce the build. Which option would you pick for a microservice that needs a preinstalled native library? keyIdea.title: Environment choice
keyIdea.text: Managed images are convenient; custom images provide full control. Pin runtime-versions for reproducibility.

content.html:
Architecture
Build environment choices
  • Managed image: quick start, maintained defaults, fewer maintenance tasks.
  • Custom image: pre-baked toolchains, full control, you manage updates and hosting.
  • runtime-versions: pin language versions like nodejs: 18 to guarantee interpreter behavior.
Test locally in a container that mirrors the environment to avoid surprises when the build runs in CodeBuild.
Decision checklist
  • Do builds require native libraries? Prefer custom images.
  • Is quick onboarding more important? Use managed images with pinned runtime-versions.
  • Will multiple teams reuse the same toolchain? Consider a curated custom image.
Pro tip

Pin both the environment image and runtime-versions to reduce surprises in CI runs.

screens.title: Service role and permissions
screens.narratorSegment: Every CodeBuild project runs with a service role — an IAM role that allows CodeBuild to interact with other AWS services. At minimum, a role typically needs permission to read source from CodeCommit or the configured source provider, to write logs to CloudWatch Logs, and to upload artifacts to an S3 bucket. A classic lab failure occurs when the auto-created role lacks s3:PutObject for your chosen artifacts bucket, producing an Access Denied during upload. The practical fix is to attach or edit an inline policy that grants s3:PutObject and related permissions limited to the artifact bucket. The chapter provides a secure example policy that scopes PutObject and GetBucketLocation to the specific bucket ARN. A common misconception is to give broad S3 permissions; prefer least privilege by scoping to the artifact bucket. After updating the role, rerun the build and confirm the artifact appears in S3. As you design roles, also consider whether the build needs additional permissions such as reading from other S3 keys or pushing to ECR for image builds. What exact permission would you add if uploads keep failing?

keyIdea.title: Permissions matter
keyIdea.text: Ensure the service role has s3:PutObject for the artifact bucket and CloudWatch Logs permissions to diagnose failures.

content.html:
Process Flow
Service role essentials
The role should include permissions to:
  • Read source (CodeCommit or other provider).
  • Write logs to CloudWatch Logs.
  • Upload artifacts to the specific S3 bucket (s3:PutObject and related actions).
Example policy snippet
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": [ "s3:PutObject", "s3:GetObject", "s3:GetObjectVersion", "s3:GetBucketAcl", "s3:GetBucketLocation" ], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:s3:::my-codebuild-artifacts-yourname/*", "arn:aws:s3:::my-codebuild-artifacts-yourname" ] } ] }
Attach minimal permissions scoped to your artifact bucket instead of AmazonS3FullAccess for safer deployments in production.

screens.title: Debugging CodeBuild failures
screens.narratorSegment: When a build fails, CloudWatch Logs is your first and best source of truth. CodeBuild streams each phase's stdout and stderr to a log group with detailed timestamps for every command executed. Start by opening the failed build's logs and locate the first error line — the command exit code or missing file often points to the root cause. For example, if npm install fails with a missing runtime, check whether runtime-versions was set correctly in buildspec. yml. If artifact upload fails with Access Denied, verify the service role includes s3:PutObject for the target bucket. Another useful tactic is to reproduce failing commands inside a local container that matches the build environment; that isolates network or dependency issues. Remember to check paths: a wrong artifacts. base-directory or wrong glob will make files seem to vanish even if the build produced them. Finally, inspect cache effectiveness by measuring build time before and after caching. After you fix the issue, run the build again and confirm logs show the error no longer occurs. What log message will you search for first when a build aborts mid-phase?

narration.text: When a build fails, CloudWatch Logs is your first and best source of truth. CodeBuild streams each phase's stdout and stderr to a log group with detailed timestamps for every command executed. Start by opening the failed build's logs and locate the first error line — the command exit code or missing file often points to the root cause. For example, if npm install fails with a missing runtime, check whether runtime-versions was set correctly in buildspec. yml. content.html:
Process
How to debug a failing build
Follow these steps:
  1. Open CloudWatch Logs for the build and find the first error line.
  2. Confirm runtime-versions and dependency installs ran successfully.
  3. Check artifacts.base-directory and the uploaded ZIP contents in S3.
  4. Verify the service role has required permissions like s3:PutObject.
Common failure patterns
  • Missing runtime: install phase didn't set the interpreter.
  • Dependency install errors: network or registry issues, or cache corruption.
  • Artifact upload Access Denied: insufficient service role permissions.
Common mistake

Assuming artifacts uploaded means build succeeded; always verify the artifact contents match expectations.

Lab Walkthrough
Create a CodeBuild project for a simple web app
Follow these commands to prepare and commit the starter files, then configure the project in the console as described in the chapter.
# index.html <!DOCTYPE html> <html> <head> <title>My CodeBuild App</title> </head> <body> <h1>Hello from CodeBuild!</h1> <p>This page was built and packaged by AWS CodeBuild.</p> </body> </html> # buildspec.yml version: 0.2 phases: build: commands: - echo "Starting build..." - echo "Copying static files to artifact directory..." - mkdir -p build_output - cp index.html build_output/ - echo "Build complete." artifacts: files: - '**/*' base-directory: 'build_output'
After committing and pushing these files, create a CodeBuild project named MySimpleWebAppBuild, set source to CodeCommit, and choose a managed image. If artifact upload fails, update the service role with s3:PutObject for your bucket.
Checklist
  1. Commit index.html and buildspec.yml to CodeCommit.
  2. Create a private S3 bucket for artifacts.
  3. Create CodeBuild project using the repository buildspec.
  4. Add s3 permissions to the service role if upload fails.
  5. Run the build and verify the ZIP in S3 contains index.html.

fullNarratorScript:
Today we'll explore AWS CodeBuild and how it automates compilation, testing, and artifact creation so teams don't maintain build servers. CodeBuild runs your commands in a managed environment or a custom Docker image and charges only for the compute time you use. You'll learn the single authoritative build file, buildspec. yml, how its install, pre_build, build, and post_build phases map to real tasks, and how artifacts and cache speed up delivery. We'll also cover the service role that gives CodeBuild permissions to access source and to publish artifacts to S3, and how CloudWatch Logs reveal step-by-step build output for debugging. As you move through this chapter, you will see concrete examples for a Node. js project, a small hands-on lab to package a static index. html, and a common IAM permission pitfall when uploading artifacts to S3. By the end, you should be able to create a CodeBuild project, author a correct buildspec. yml, and fix the common access denied errors by adjusting the service role. What build step will you try first in your repository?

These objectives focus on practical, verifiable skills you can perform with CodeBuild. You will configure a CodeBuild project to compile source, run tests, and produce artifacts suitable for deployment. You will read and author buildspec. yml files and place commands into the correct phases so builds run reliably. You will use environment variables, caching, and service roles to make builds faster and secure. You will integrate CodeBuild with source providers like CodeCommit and with S3 for artifact storage. Finally, you will analyze build logs in CloudWatch to locate and fix failures, including typical permission errors when uploading artifacts. Each objective is a clear, testable milestone: create a project, commit a working buildspec, verify artifacts in S3, and diagnose a failing build using logs. These are the skills that will let you operate CI pipelines without guessing why a build failed.

This second objectives slide breaks the chapter into demonstrable tasks you can perform and be tested on. You will commit a buildspec. yml that uses runtime-versions and a clear base-directory for artifacts, then run a build and confirm artifacts land in an S3 bucket. You will inspect CloudWatch Logs to identify a failing build command, and you will update the service role to add s3 permissions to fix Access Denied errors. You will also set up caching for npm or Maven to reduce build minutes. Finally, you will understand the managed versus custom build environment choice: managed images give safe defaults; custom images let you pre-bake toolchains. These objectives are concrete: write, push, run, inspect logs, and correct permissions. Achieving them shows you can operate and troubleshoot CodeBuild pipelines beyond just reading configuration files.

Start with a simple claim: CodeBuild is a fully managed continuous integration service that runs your build commands and produces artifacts without provisioning build servers. That means you describe what to do in a buildspec. yml and CodeBuild runs it in a managed environment or a custom Docker image you provide. A concrete example: you commit a Node. js project to CodeCommit and configure CodeBuild to run npm install, npm run build, and npm test; CodeBuild executes those commands and uploads the output to S3. A common misconception is that CodeBuild supplies persistent state between builds. It does not — builds are ephemeral. To persist dependencies across builds you use the cache feature or an artifacts bucket. Another contrast: managed images provide common runtimes preinstalled, while custom images let you bake in specialized tools. Why this matters: choosing the right environment affects reproducibility and first-run failures. Key questions to ask when designing a build are what commands must run, where artifacts should go, and which IAM permissions are needed. Practice by writing a minimal buildspec. yml and running a single build — that will reveal whether your runtime and paths are correct. How would you make your first build deterministic?

The buildspec. yml is the instruction set CodeBuild follows. Treat it as a sequence of phases: install, pre_build, build, and post_build. Put runtime installs and dependency managers in install — for example, installing Node. js runtime or running npm install so subsequent steps can use installed packages. Use pre_build for validation steps such as linting or authentication actions. The build phase contains the core compile or package commands like npm run build or mvn package. Use post_build for tasks that prepare artifacts, run integration tests, or signal downstream systems. A concrete example: in a Node. js pipeline you would set runtime-versions. nodejs, run npm install in install, npm run lint in pre_build, npm run build in build, and npm test in post_build. A common mistake is placing dependency downloads in pre_build; if the runtime isn't present earlier, commands fail. Also be explicit with artifacts. base-directory so produced files end up where CodeBuild expects. Correctly placing steps reduces first-run failures and makes logs easier to interpret. What single change would you make if your tests fail because dependencies are missing? Understanding buildspec.yml phases means install tools and runtimes in install, run checks in pre_build, compile/package in build, and finalize artifacts or tests in post_build.. In practical terms, install, pre_build, build, and post_build — what belongs where. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through a practical Node. js buildspec and explain each section. The file starts with version: 0.2 then declares phases. Under install we set runtime-versions. nodejs to 18 and run npm install, which prepares node_modules for later steps. In pre_build we run lint to catch style issues early. The build phase runs npm run build to produce production-ready files, typically in a dist directory. Post_build runs tests, and if they succeed the artifacts block tells CodeBuild to collect files under base-directory: 'dist' and upload them to S3. Cache paths such as /root/. npm/** preserve npm packages between builds to reduce time and cost. A concrete example is the buildspec used in this chapter; it installs, lints, builds, tests, and caches npm. A frequent error is incorrect base-directory or glob patterns that exclude files; verify your build created the expected folder before trusting the artifact upload. Another trap is forgetting to add s3 permissions to the service role, leading to Access Denied when uploading artifacts. After running one build, inspect CloudWatch Logs to confirm each phase ran as intended. How will you validate the artifact contains the files you expect?

Artifacts and cache both persist data between steps or builds, but they serve different purposes. Artifacts are the final outputs you intend to deploy or store — packaged files uploaded to S3 after a successful build, defined via artifacts. files and a base-directory. Cache preserves intermediate dependencies or build outputs between runs to speed subsequent builds, for example caching /root/. npm to avoid re-downloading packages. Use artifacts when you need reproducible deployables; use cache to reduce build time and cost. A common mistake is treating cache as a replacement for artifacts. Cache is optional and may be pruned; artifacts are the canonical build outputs. Another frequent error is incorrect glob patterns in artifacts. files, which omit files from uploads. To validate, always inspect the build output directory before upload and check the S3 ZIP contents. If you see Access Denied uploading artifacts, check the CodeBuild service role for s3:PutObject permission scoped to the artifact bucket. Which files in your build should be artifacts and which should be cached? Artifacts and Cache Explained means artifacts = deployable outputs in s3; cache = performance optimization for dependency reuse between builds.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Choosing an environment determines which runtimes and tools are available during a build. Managed images provide standard runtimes and are a quick way to get started. They are maintained by the provider and include common SDKs and tools. Custom Docker images let you preinstall exactly the toolchain your builds need, so builds start faster and behave identically across runs. In buildspec. yml you can also declare runtime-versions to pin language runtimes such as nodejs: 18 so commands run against a predictable interpreter. A concrete trade-off: managed images reduce maintenance but might lack niche tooling; custom images require you to build and host the image but give full control. Always test your build commands inside the chosen environment locally or in a container to catch missing tools early. Remember to document which image and runtime-version your project relies on so others can reproduce the build. Which option would you pick for a microservice that needs a preinstalled native library? Every CodeBuild project runs with a service role — an IAM role that allows CodeBuild to interact with other AWS services. At minimum, a role typically needs permission to read source from CodeCommit or the configured source provider, to write logs to CloudWatch Logs, and to upload artifacts to an S3 bucket. A classic lab failure occurs when the auto-created role lacks s3:PutObject for your chosen artifacts bucket, producing an Access Denied during upload. The chapter provides a secure example policy that scopes PutObject and GetBucketLocation to the specific bucket ARN. A common misconception is to give broad S3 permissions; prefer least privilege by scoping to the artifact bucket. After updating the role, rerun the build and confirm the artifact appears in S3. As you design roles, also consider whether the build needs additional permissions such as reading from other S3 keys or pushing to ECR for image builds.
